# Command line

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen_cli_reference.py. Do not edit by hand. -->

`interlock` (also `python -m interlock`) is installed with the package. Each
command's `--help` shows the same text as below. `--no-color` (before the
command) turns off color; color is also off when output isn't a terminal or
`NO_COLOR` is set.

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| [`doctor`](#interlock-doctor) | check that protection is actually on |
| [`report`](#interlock-report) | summarize a receipt log: blocks, monitor findings, latency |
| [`hook`](#interlock-hook) | decide one coding-agent tool call (run by the agent) |
| [`install-hook`](#interlock-install-hook) | put interlock in front of Claude Code, Codex or Cursor |
| [`policy`](#interlock-policy) | check a declarative policy file, or show a built-in pack |
| [`learn`](#interlock-learn) | draft a reviewable policy from observed receipts |
| [`trust`](#interlock-trust) | trust a project's policy overlay |
| [`mcp`](#interlock-mcp) | inventory the MCP servers configured on this machine |
| [`reviews`](#interlock-reviews) | decide pending reviews; serve their status to agents |
| [`drift`](#interlock-drift) | diff a live surface's tool listing against a recorded corpus |
| [`mesh`](#interlock-mesh) | subscribe to community policy packs, or publish a commons |

## `interlock doctor`

Check that interlock protection is actually on.

Runs host-level checks and, when you point it at them, checks your policy,
your sidecar and your receipt log:

```bash
interlock doctor
interlock doctor --rules myapp.policy:RULES --receipts audit.jsonl --key-file audit.key
interlock doctor --sidecar ~/.interlock/guard.sock --json
```

Inside your own process, call interlock.posture.attest() (or require()) instead:
it sees the installed engine, sink, guards and approver directly.

Exit codes: 0 enforced, 1 degraded (warnings), 2 unprotected (a check failed).

```text
usage: interlock doctor [-h] [--rules MODULE:ATTR] [--policy FILE] [--sidecar PATH]
                        [--receipts FILE] [--key-file FILE] [--json]
  --rules                    load this policy (same spec as interlock-sidecar --rules)
  --policy                   load this declarative policy file (JSON, or YAML with PyYAML)
  --sidecar                  probe the sidecar listening on this socket
  --receipts                 check this receipt log
  --key-file                 the receipt MAC key, to verify the log's chain
  --json                     machine-readable output
```

## `interlock report`

Summarize a receipt log: what interlock blocked, rewrote and escalated, what
monitor mode would have done, how long evaluation took, and whether any
receipts were lost.

```bash
interlock report audit.jsonl --key-file audit.key
interlock report audit.jsonl --since 24h --monitor     # "would have blocked"
interlock report audit.jsonl --json
```

The chain is verified first when --key-file is given; the report always says
whether it was. Receipts hold argument digests, never values.

Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 the chain is broken, 3 the log could not be read.

```text
usage: interlock report [-h] [--since DURATION] [--monitor] [--top N] [--key-file FILE] [--json]
                        file
  file                       a receipt log written by FileSink
  --since                    only receipts newer than this: 30m, 24h, 7d (default: all)
  --monitor                  show what monitor mode would have blocked or rewritten
  --top                      rows per table
  --key-file                 the MAC key, to verify the chain
  --json                     machine-readable output
```

## `interlock hook`

Decide one coding-agent tool call (run by the agent, not by you).

The agent passes its hook payload on stdin; the verdict goes back on stdout and
the exit code, in that agent's own protocol. `interlock install-hook` writes
the command line; you do not normally run this by hand, except to test:

```bash
echo '{"hook_event_name":"PreToolUse","tool_name":"Bash",
       "tool_input":{"command":"git push --force origin main"},
       "session_id":"s","cwd":"/tmp"}' | interlock hook --agent claude-code
```

Any error - unreadable input, a policy that will not load, a crash - denies the
call (fail closed) unless --on-error allow, which lets the call through and
says so loudly.

```text
usage: interlock hook [-h] --agent {claude-code,codex,cursor} [--policy FILE]
                      [--rules MODULE:ATTR] [--sidecar PATH] [--receipts FILE] [--key-file FILE]
                      [--no-receipts] [--no-overlay] [--monitor] [--on-error {deny,allow}]
                      [--reviews {fallback,always,off}] [--review-db FILE]
  --agent                    
  --policy                   policy file (default ~/.interlock/policy.json, else the built-in coding-agent pack)
  --rules                    a Python policy module instead
  --sidecar                  ask this sidecar instead
  --receipts                 receipt log (default ~/.interlock/receipts.jsonl when its key exists)
  --key-file                 receipt MAC key
  --no-receipts              write no receipts
  --no-overlay               ignore project overlays
  --monitor                  record what would happen, never block
  --on-error                 what an internal error does (default deny)
  --reviews                  settle escalations through the review queue: when the agent can't ask (default), always, or never
  --review-db                review queue (default ~/.interlock/reviews.db)
```

## `interlock install-hook`

Put interlock in front of a coding agent's tool calls.

```bash
interlock install-hook --for claude-code
interlock install-hook --for all --dry-run       # show the change, write nothing
interlock install-hook --for codex --uninstall
```

Registers `interlock hook --agent <name>` in the agent's hook settings
(~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.codex/hooks.json, ~/.cursor/hooks.json), keeping
every other entry, backing the file up first (<file>.interlock-bak) and
replacing any earlier interlock entry. The hook runs this Python and this
interlock package, whatever directory the agent runs it from, and denies the
call if it cannot start. It also creates ~/.interlock with a default policy
that extends the built-in coding-agent pack and a key for the receipt log.
Restart running agent sessions afterwards; re-run this if interlock moves.

Run this yourself, outside the agent: the coding-agent pack refuses it from
inside one.

Exit codes: 0 done, 1 an agent could not be configured, 64 bad arguments.

```text
usage: interlock install-hook [-h] --for {claude-code,codex,cursor,all} [--settings FILE]
                              [--policy FILE] [--sidecar PATH] [--receipts FILE] [--key-file FILE]
                              [--monitor] [--dry-run] [--uninstall]
  --for                      
  --settings                 the agent's settings file (default: its usual path)
  --policy                   pin this policy file in the hook
  --sidecar                  decide through this sidecar
  --receipts                 receipt log path
  --key-file                 receipt key path
  --monitor                  install in monitor mode
  --dry-run                  print the change only
  --uninstall                remove interlock's hooks
```

## `interlock policy`

Check a declarative policy file before you rely on it.

```bash
interlock policy check policy.json
interlock policy check ~/.interlock/policy.json --overlay .interlock/policy.json
interlock policy show builtin:coding-agent        # print a built-in pack
```

`check` loads the file the way the guard will: it lists the rules, the locked
ones, any rule quarantined as invalid (with why), and each overlay's status.

Exit codes: 0 valid, 1 loaded with quarantined rules, 2 does not load.

```text
usage: interlock policy [-h] ACTION ...
usage: interlock policy check [-h] [--overlay FILE] [--json] file
usage: interlock policy show [-h] name
```

## `interlock learn`

Draft a reviewable policy from a receipt log: the actions your guard
actually allowed, and an escalation for everything else.

```bash
interlock learn --receipts audit.jsonl --out baseline.json
interlock learn --receipts audit.jsonl --out baseline.json --name acme-baseline
```

Reads a receipt log written by FileSink, keeps the actions observed with an
ALLOW verdict (matched case-insensitively), and writes a declarative policy
whose single rule escalates any action outside that envelope. The draft is
deterministic - two runs over the same log are byte-identical - so a diff
between two drafts is worth reviewing.

It is never auto-enforced: this command only writes the file you name. It
installs nothing, enables nothing, locks nothing and emits no `block` rule.
Review it with `interlock policy check` and install it on purpose.

Exit codes: 0 wrote the policy, 3 the log could not be read, held no
ALLOW-observed receipt, or the output could not be written (no file is written
in those cases); 64 the command line was wrong.

```text
usage: interlock learn [-h] [--receipts FILE] [--out FILE] [--name NAME]
  --receipts                 a receipt log written by FileSink (required)
  --out                      where to write the draft policy (required)
  --name                     the policy 'name' field (default: learned-behavioural-baseline)
```

## `interlock trust`

Trust (or stop trusting) a project's policy overlay.

```bash
interlock trust add                 # the overlay found from this directory
interlock trust add path/to/.interlock/policy.json
interlock trust list                # ok / CHANGED / MISSING
interlock trust remove [PATH]
```

An overlay (.interlock/policy.json in a repository) is ignored until trusted,
and trust is tied to the file's exact content: edit it and it is ignored again
until you re-trust it. `add` shows what the overlay adds before recording it.
Run this yourself, outside the agent - the coding-agent pack refuses it from
inside one.

```text
usage: interlock trust [-h] [--store FILE] ACTION ...
  --store                    trust file (default ~/.interlock/trusted.json)
usage: interlock trust add [-h] [--yes] [path]
usage: interlock trust list [-h]
usage: interlock trust remove [-h] [path]
```

## `interlock mcp`

Inventory the MCP servers configured on this machine.

```bash
interlock mcp scan                       # every server, with risk notes
interlock mcp scan --json
interlock mcp scan --emit-policy mcp.json  # a rule blocking unlisted servers
interlock mcp where github               # every config that defines it
```

Reads Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and
Codex configs (user scope, plus the project around --cwd). Never starts a server
and never touches the network. Environment and header values are not read into
the report - only their names.

Exit codes: 0 no risks found, 1 at least one risk note, 2 nothing matched (where).

```text
usage: interlock mcp [-h] ACTION ...
usage: interlock mcp scan [-h] [--json] [--cwd CWD] [--emit-policy FILE]
usage: interlock mcp where [-h] [--cwd CWD] name
```

## `interlock reviews`

Decide pending reviews, and serve their status to agents.

```bash
interlock reviews list                   # pending first; --status, --all
interlock reviews show r-1a2b3c4d
interlock reviews approve r-1a2b3c4d     # --as NAME (default: your login)
interlock reviews reject r-1a2b3c4d --reason "use the staging table"
interlock reviews revoke r-1a2b3c4d
interlock reviews wait r-1a2b3c4d --timeout 120
interlock reviews mcp                    # read-only MCP server (stdio)
```

A review is filed when a call escalates and is settled through the queue (see
interlock.reviews). After an approval the agent retries the identical call,
which runs once. Run approve/reject/revoke yourself, outside the agent: the
coding-agent policy refuses them from inside one.

For the agent, add the MCP server to its config, e.g. for Claude Code:
```bash
{"mcpServers": {"interlock-reviews": {"command": "interlock", "args": ["reviews", "mcp"]}}}
```

Exit codes: 0 done, 1 the review can't be changed (wrong state, self-approval,
unknown id), 64 bad arguments.

```text
usage: interlock reviews [-h] [--db FILE] [--json] ACTION ...
  --db                       review queue (default ~/.interlock/reviews.db)
  --json                     machine-readable output
usage: interlock reviews list [-h] [--status {pending,approved,rejected,revoked,expired,executed}]
                              [--limit LIMIT]
usage: interlock reviews show [-h] id
usage: interlock reviews approve [-h] [--as NAME] id
usage: interlock reviews reject [-h] [--as NAME] [--reason REASON] id
usage: interlock reviews revoke [-h] [--as NAME] id
usage: interlock reviews wait [-h] [--timeout TIMEOUT] id
usage: interlock reviews mcp [-h]
```

## `interlock drift`

Diff a live surface's tool listing against a recorded corpus.

```bash
interlock drift --corpus corpus.json --live "my-mcp-server --list-tools"
interlock drift --corpus corpus.json --live "..." --surface demo
interlock drift --corpus corpus.json --live "..." --json
```

The corpus records each covered surface's tool-listing fingerprint and schema
shapes (see ``interlock/drift.py``). ``--live`` runs a command and reads its
standard output as the live tool listing: one tool name per line, or one JSON
object per line when you also record schema shapes. ``--live`` is a shell
string, so a command with arguments or quoted paths works as written.

Every added tool, removed tool and changed schema shape is reported with a
severity, and any finding is drift. **Nothing is written back and nothing is
filed** - the corpus is only ever read - so the diff is a report you act on.

Exit codes: 0 no drift, 1 drift found, 64 the command line was wrong,
3 the corpus could not be read or the live command failed.

```text
usage: interlock drift [-h] [--corpus FILE] [--live CMD] [--surface NAME] [--json]
  --corpus                   the recorded corpus to diff against
  --live                     a shell command whose stdout is the live tool listing
  --surface                  which corpus surface the live command describes (default: the corpus's only surface)
  --json                     machine-readable output
```

## `interlock mesh`

Subscribe to the interlock mesh, or publish a commons for it.

For a node (the deployment running an agent):

```bash
interlock mesh init --root root.json --mirror https://commons.example.org [--ring stable]
interlock mesh sync                       # fetch and verify; the cache only changes if all of it verifies
interlock mesh status [--json]            # subscriptions, freshness, what shadow rules would have done
interlock mesh resolve mesh:coding-agent@stable   # print the pack as this node would install it
```

Then in your policy file:  {"version": 1, "extends": "mesh:coding-agent@stable", "rules": [...]}

For a maintainer (the people who run a commons):

```bash
interlock mesh keys init --out keys/      # one Ed25519 key per role; raise counts/thresholds for a real root
interlock mesh publish --source commons/ --out site/ --keys keys/
interlock mesh verify site/               # walk the site exactly as a subscriber would
```

A node never auto-enforces a new community rule: every rule it has not seen
before spends a monitor window in shadow mode, and a rule's status and the
node's ring cap how strong its verdict may be. See docs/guides/mesh.md.

Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 the mesh is stale or a shadow summary shows findings
(status), 2 verification or publishing failed, 3 a file could not be read,
64 the command line was wrong.

```text
usage: interlock mesh [-h] ACTION ...
usage: interlock mesh init [-h] --root FILE [--mirror URL] [--ring {canary,early,stable}]
                           [--monitor-days DAYS] [--dir DIR]
usage: interlock mesh sync [-h] [--dir DIR] [--json]
usage: interlock mesh status [-h] [--dir DIR] [--json]
usage: interlock mesh resolve [-h] [--dir DIR] spec
usage: interlock mesh keys [-h] ACTION ...
usage: interlock mesh publish [-h] --source DIR --out DIR --keys DIR [--timestamp-days DAYS]
                              [--no-validate] [--json]
usage: interlock mesh verify [-h] [--root FILE] [--json] DIR
usage: interlock mesh report [-h] ACTION ...
usage: interlock mesh serve [-h] --role {consensus,aggregator,mirror} [--bind HOST:PORT]
                            [--state FILE] [--token TOKEN] [--known-catalog ID] [--min-orgs N]
                            [--dir DIR] [--require-credential] [--issuer HEX_PUBLIC]
                            [--min-batch N]
usage: interlock mesh log [-h] [--root FILE] [--json] DIR_OR_URL
usage: interlock mesh gossip [-h] --peer URL [--dir DIR] [--token TOKEN]
usage: interlock mesh credential [-h] ACTION ...
usage: interlock mesh harness [-h] --policy FILE --benign FILE [--samples FILE]
                              [--max-fp-rate RATE] [--max-p95-us US] [--min-recall RATE] [--json]
usage: interlock mesh forge [-h] --state FILE --benign FILE --out DIR [--samples FILE]
                            [--max-fp-rate RATE] [--min-recall RATE]
usage: interlock mesh consensus [-h] ACTION ...
```
